claims.text: The baseline is a W–Mo–Nb–Ta-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The intervention substitutes approximately 5–10 at% aluminum for part of the heavier alloying elements.
Adding 5–10 at% aluminum will induce nanoscale ordered precipitates.
The aluminum-induced precipitates may have an L1_2 structure.
The nanoscale ordered precipitates will be uniformly distributed in the matrix.
Aluminum promotes a precipitation reaction during controlled heat treatment.
The precipitates impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
Impeded dislocation motion will enhance high-temperature yield strength.
The precipitates will improve high-temperature creep resistance.
Substitution of heavier elements with aluminum will reduce the alloy's overall density.
The aluminum-modified alloy will retain substantially unchanged room-temperature mechanical performance.
At approximately 900°C, the aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit a 20–30% increase in yield strength relative to the aluminum-free baseline.
Alternatively, the aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit improved creep resistance at approximately 900°C.
Room-temperature yield strength will remain within ±10% of the baseline value.
Room-temperature ductility will remain within ±10% of the baseline value.
The predicted improvement applies near 900°C under low to moderate strain rates.
The improvement may not persist in extreme environments where the precipitates become unstable.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits improved creep resistance as an alternative to a 20–30% yield-strength increase, but the falsification rule requires at least a 20% yield-strength increase. Thus, a material showing improved creep resistance without the specified yield-strength increase could satisfy the prediction yet be declared refuted.
